articles.title: From vacant plots to valuable land: Berlin's property boom pinches its 'underground' culture
articles.summary: Berlin's rising rents and soaring property prices are squeezing the city's underground culture, from DIY bars and open-air discos to alternative
articles.body: Berlin's rising rents and soaring property prices are squeezing the city's underground culture, from DIY bars and open-air discos to alternative performance spaces that have long operated on vacant plots, old industrial sites and other unused land.This underground scene, built around informal venues, artists' collectives and community-run spaces, has been closely tied to Berlin's history of making use of abandoned and inexpensive properties. But as land values rise and cheap or unused spaces become harder to find, some of the venues that helped shape the city's alternative identity are being forced to move or shut down.Residential property prices in Berlin have more than tripled over the past 15 years, while the city's supply of relatively cheap or unused spaces has steadily shrunk. The squeeze is now threatening some of the informal venues and communities that have long been part of Berlin's urban identity.One example is "die Greife", a stretch of vacant land in northeast Berlin near the Prenzlauer Berg neighbourhood that has been used by alternative groups for bars, open-air discos and performance spaces.Zirkus Mond, an alternative circus troupe, has operated on the site for eight years. But the developer that had allowed the group to use the land now wants it back, forcing the troupe to move."It's sad but we knew it was going to come, and we found another place," said Max Mohr, director of Zirkus Mond, as reported by Reuters.The troupe, which includes jugglers, dancers and acrobats, had previously staged shows in abandoned buildings before settling at the site. Over the past decade, groups including Kollage Kollektiv, Jonny Knueppel and Mucha gradually transformed the previously unused stretch of land into a cluster of cultural and social spaces."This type of space used to be common in Berlin," said Elva Lebrun from the Mucha association. "It's also part of the essence and identity of Berlin, raw and also DIY – everything you see here is done by us."The loss of such spaces reflects a broader change in Berlin's property market. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, artists and alternative communities moved into vacant warehouses, industrial buildings and unused plots across the city, often paying relatively little for large amounts of space.That availability helped establish Berlin's reputation as a relatively affordable destination for artists and young people, while giving unused urban land a new purpose.But as the German capital has grown, land has become more valuable and the amount of space available for temporary or informal use has declined.The pressure is also being felt in the residential market. Housing costs have risen sharply, making it harder for some of the people who were once drawn to Berlin's alternative scene to afford to remain in the city.Juan Migama, the Spanish-born artistic director of Zirkus Mond, said the cost of housing was driving away some people who had previously been attracted to Berlin, although he said the city remained tolerant and open-minded.The property squeeze has become a major political issue in Berlin. A far-left party won a state election last month after campaigning on a pledge to take housing from corporate landlords and cap rents.Berlin's relationship with alternative communities has historically been shaped by its unusual property landscape. During the Cold War, students, punks and hippies occupied spaces in West Berlin, while the years after reunification brought a new wave of artists into vacant buildings and former industrial sites.Even the city's bureaucracy has sometimes helped such projects survive. Interim-use rules allowed diskoBabel, the association operating "die Greife", to use the vacant land, despite the site having no running water and relying on generators for electricity.The arrangement illustrates the precarious nature of many such spaces: they can operate while land remains unused, but their future changes once a developer decides to reclaim the property."Germans have a lot of rules, it's true. And because they have so many rules, they have rules that make these things possible," Migama said. "You can be in a kind of grey area, but as soon as you follow those rules, they let you be."For groups operating on temporary sites, however, rising property values mean that finding another space is becoming increasingly difficult."It is not a recipe for getting rich but people living outside the mainstream have always needed to overcome obstacles," Mohr said. "If you want this lifestyle, you have to be very driven. It's maybe a lot of work, but it is possible to do this."Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: 'Very heavy price': Netanyahu warns of retaliation if flydubai co-pilot was acting on orders
articles.summary: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that the suspected attacker aboard a flydubai flight had undergone Islamist radicalization and
articles.body: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that the suspected attacker aboard a flydubai flight had undergone Islamist radicalization and intended to crash the aircraft with its passengers on board, warning that "whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price". The remarks come as investigators examine whether the assault on Indian Captain Smit Machchhar was directed by an outside party."As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer. Yaniv and his heroic companions prevented a disaster on the scale of 9/11. The attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He intended to crash the plane with all its passengers on board," Netanyahu said."We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price", the PM added.The comments came after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed Machchhar aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday. The aircraft, carrying 174 people, plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the situation was brought under control.Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. Two off-duty Flydubai pilots who were on board then helped take control of the aircraft, which landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.READ ALSO: 'Exceptional courage': Pilots body writes to PM Modi, requests bravery award for Smit MachchharNetanyahu had earlier said the attacker was being interrogated and that Israeli investigators had joined the questioning."The attacker, the co-pilot who attacked the captain, is now being interrogated. What we know so far is that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," Netanyahu told Fox News.He also said the initial investigation suggested the co-pilot was suicidal."He is lying on the floor and he calls out to the crew 'kill me, kill me'. So, it is clear that he was suicidal and was going to down the plane," Netanyahu said.However, the motive and any possible outside involvement have not been conclusively established. The UAE has launched an investigation into the circumstances and motives. Earlier, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash described the cockpit attack as a “dangerous terrorist act”.“The Indian pilot at Flydubai, Smit Machchhar, deserves all the appreciation, as he embodied the true meaning of courage and responsibility when confronting a dangerous terrorist act and a potential disaster,” Gargash stated.Additionally, Israel’s Consul General in Mumbai, Yaniv Revach, also condemned the incident as an act of terror. Speaking to ANI, Revach said, “First of all, I don't think that it might be a terror attack. It is a terror attack. So there's not even a question or a doubt about it.” He also expressed gratitude for Machchhar’s “exceptional behaviour”.READ ALSO: 'Terrorist act': UAE official on flydubai attack, praises India pilot Smit MachchharNetanyahu has also praised Machchhar and the passengers who intervened. "I think what happened is a tremendous act of heroism that prevented another 9/11 style crash of an entire airplane," he told CBS News.Machchhar, who is recovering in Abu Dhabi, later spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi by video call. Recalling the moment the aircraft began losing altitude, he said: "I knew that the aircraft was going down ... I had fallen to the ground. I told myself that the door is right there, just open it. I managed to do it and people entered."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Why Kaliningrad matters to Putin: The Suwałki Gap vulnerability, Kremlin's nuclear threat and India link
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned that Moscow could use “all weapons” in its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if its Baltic exclave of
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned that Moscow could use “all weapons” in its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under direct attack. The warning has brought renewed attention to a narrow stretch of land between Poland and Lithuania, known as the Suwałki Gap, which lies between Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus and is considered a potential flashpoint in a conflict between Russia and Nato.Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country but would respond if the West escalated tensions or threatened Russian territory. He referred to Nato military activity in the Baltic region, attempts to intercept Russian ships and statements about Kaliningrad.“The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said.“If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” he cautioned.The remarks followed a Russian diplomatic warning that Moscow could resort to nuclear weapons if Nato attempted to cut off Kaliningrad by land, air or sea. Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the alliance was defensive and urged Russia to stop its nuclear rhetoric. He also said there was no immediate threat to Nato territory from Russia.Why Kaliningrad matters to RussiaKaliningrad is a heavily militarised Russian territory separated from the country’s mainland. It is located between Poland and Lithuania, both Nato members, and has a coastline on the Baltic Sea. The region has a population of about one million and is slightly larger than the US state of Connecticut.The territory was formerly known as Königsberg and was the capital of East Prussia. It became part of the Soviet Union after the Red Army captured it in April 1945, towards the end of World War II. The victorious Allied powers subsequently divided East Prussia, and the northern part, including Königsberg, came under Soviet control. The city was later renamed Kaliningrad.Its location gives Moscow a military foothold on the Baltic Sea, far from the Russian mainland but close to several Nato countries. Kaliningrad provides a base for Russian air defence, missile and naval forces, allowing Moscow to project military power into northern and central Europe.That strategic value also creates a vulnerability. Since the region is separated from mainland Russia by the territory of other countries, Moscow would face logistical challenges in supplying or reinforcing it during a conflict. Its land borders are with Poland and Lithuania, while access to the Baltic Sea is subject to the military and political situation in the region.Kaliningrad’s position has become more sensitive since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Nato has strengthened its eastern flank, while Finland and Sweden joined the alliance in 2023 and 2024 respectively. Their membership has altered the security environment around the Baltic Sea and added to Moscow’s concerns about the alliance’s military presence in the region.The Suwałki Gap vulnerabilityThe Suwałki Gap is a narrow stretch of land, around 60 miles long, along the Poland-Lithuania border. It separates Kaliningrad from Belarus, a close Russian ally. It is also the land corridor connecting the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania with the rest of Nato.The corridor has acquired strategic importance because of what could happen if Russia gained control of it. A Russian military advance through the gap could potentially link Kaliningrad with Belarus and disrupt the land connection between the Baltic states and other Nato members.Also read: What's Suwalki gap? Europe's 'achilles heel' that it fears could be Putin's targetSuch a move would place Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in a more isolated position during a conflict. Their security depends on the ability of Nato forces to move personnel, equipment and supplies through Poland and Lithuania. The Suwałki Gap is therefore viewed by security analysts as a vulnerable point in the alliance’s eastern defences.The gap is not, however, an established route for an imminent Russian operation. Any attempt to seize it would mean a direct military confrontation with Poland and Lithuania, and therefore with Nato. The possibility is one of the reasons the corridor features prominently in military planning and discussions about the defence of the Baltic states.For Moscow, Kaliningrad is both a military asset and a territory that could become difficult to defend if a conflict disrupted its access routes. For Nato, the Suwałki Gap is important because it links the Baltic members of the alliance to the rest of the bloc. This geography makes the region a potential flashpoint, even without an active military confrontation.What has triggered the latest tensions?Tensions around Kaliningrad have increased as Nato has strengthened its presence in the Baltic region following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly criticised Western military activity near the exclave and described comments by European officials about Kaliningrad as threatening.In May 2026, Russia condemned remarks by Lithuania’s foreign minister, who said Nato had to demonstrate that it could penetrate what he described as the “small fortress” built by Russia in Kaliningrad and destroy its air defences and missile bases.A Western military source told Reuters that dozens of aircraft from Nato countries took part in an unannounced operation in the airspace around Kaliningrad in mid-August. The operation reportedly demonstrated the alliance’s ability to disrupt the exclave’s radio and radar links, as well as its air defences, in the event of a conflict.Nato has said its increased presence in the Baltic Sea is partly a response to concerns over threats to critical undersea energy and communications infrastructure. The alliance has also cited the need to strengthen deterrence along its eastern flank.Russia, meanwhile, has accused Nato of escalating tensions and has used diplomatic statements and social media posts by its embassies to draw attention to what it describes as threatening military movements and rhetoric. The alliance has rejected the suggestion that it intends to attack or isolate Kaliningrad.Why a crisis could escalateAnalysts have warned that a direct confrontation between Russia and Nato could emerge from a miscalculation rather than a planned attack. Kaliningrad’s location makes it particularly sensitive to incidents involving military aircraft, drones, naval vessels or critical infrastructure.Possible triggers include a drone incident, disruption of undersea infrastructure, new missile deployments or an action that Moscow interprets as an attempt to impose a blockade on the exclave. A dispute over access to Kaliningrad could also intensify if military movements in the Baltic Sea or around the Suwałki Gap were misread by either side.Since 2022, European countries have supported Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and sanctions against Russia while avoiding direct participation in the war. Moscow has accused Western countries of effectively waging war against it, a charge rejected by Nato members.Putin’s warning over Kaliningrad comes amid this wider confrontation. It does not establish that Russia has decided to use nuclear weapons, but it underlines Moscow’s willingness to invoke its nuclear arsenal in response to what it describes as a direct attack on Russian territory.Nato has said it does not threaten Kaliningrad and has described Russia’s nuclear warnings as irresponsible. Rutte said the alliance had responded calmly to Moscow’s warning and reiterated its defensive position.Ukraine war adds to pressure on MoscowPutin’s comments on Kaliningrad came as Russia’s war in Ukraine entered its fifth year. Moscow has continued its offensive and intensified attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and Kyiv ahead of winter.Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and other targets deep inside Russian territory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described such strikes as “long-range sanctions”, aimed at reducing Russia’s revenue and military capacity and pushing the Kremlin towards negotiations.Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries had affected the country’s economy. He said the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of its gross domestic product. He also said Ukrainian military operations in the Black Sea had damaged or destroyed more than 100 Russian ships.“In the Black Sea — that’s a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now we’re being bombarded from every direction with appeals: “Oh, please stop doing that,” Putin said.“It’s the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially — by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately — these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,” Putin added.His remarks came a day after he told newly elected members of Russia’s State Duma that the country’s economy was stable. He also criticised Ukraine’s reliance on financial assistance from Western allies, saying Russia did not need external handouts.“Mistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,” he warned parliamentarians. “Unlike some, and we won’t point fingers, Russia can’t run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” he said.Putin has said he would prefer the war to end through negotiations, but has not indicated that Moscow is prepared to withdraw from its military objectives. A Levada Center poll in August found that 59% of Russians favoured moving towards peace talks.Russia’s planned defence spending also points to a continued military commitment. Budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Moscow plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles ($205.112 billion) on defence in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.India's military connection to KaliningradBeyond its strategic importance in European security, Kaliningrad has a direct defence connection with India through the Russian Yantar Shipyard.Located in the exclave, Yantar has built several warships for the Indian Navy, including two upgraded Talwar-class frigates, INS Tushil and INS Tamal. Both vessels were constructed in Russia and commissioned into the Indian Navy at Kaliningrad.INS Tushil was launched at Yantar Shipyard on October 28, 2021, and commissioned in December 2024. INS Tamal, the second frigate under the project, was commissioned at the same facility on July 1, 2025.The two vessels are part of a four-frigate arrangement between India and Russia under Project 1135.6. The agreement involves constructing two ships in Russia and two in India, with technology transfer and design assistance from the Russian side.The commissioning of INS Tamal marked the completion of the Russian-built portion of the project. However, India's naval cooperation with Russia has not ended with the delivery of these two warships.The remaining two frigates, INS Triput and INS Tavasya, are being constructed at Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) in India.The first vessel, Triput, was launched on July 23, 2024, while Tavasya was launched on March 22, 2025. Both are based on the Project 1135.6 design and are intended to undertake surface, sub-surface and air combat operations.The ships are 124.8 metres long, have a displacement of approximately 3,600 tonnes and can achieve a maximum speed of 28 knots.Their construction represents India's transition from directly procuring warships from Russia to manufacturing them domestically with foreign design assistance.The ministry of defence has described the project as part of India's efforts to strengthen indigenous warship construction. The vessels incorporate a large percentage of Indian-origin equipment, weapons and sensors. These include localised components such as the BrahMos missile system, torpedo launchers, sonar and auxiliary control systems.Is India still dependent on Kaliningrad?India is no longer receiving complete frigates from Kaliningrad under this particular project. However, the Russian connection continues through the technology transfer and design assistance arrangement for the two ships being constructed in Goa.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The Rashtriya Rifles: The temporary force that stayed 36 years
articles.summary: The Rashtriya Rifles was raised as a force that could be wound up by executive order.
articles.body: The Rashtriya Rifles was raised as a force that could be wound up by executive order. Thirty-six years later, it is among the Indian Army’s most decorated formations.Indian governments have a particular talent for the permanent temporary arrangement. The Calcutta tram, which has spent most of my adult life apparently months away from abolition, is one example. The Rashtriya Rifles is another, though rather better armed.When it was raised on 1 October 1990, with six battalions - three sent to Punjab, three to Jammu and Kashmir - the RR was constituted under a provision of the Union Composite Table that allowed it to be disbanded by executive order. Thirty-six years, roughly 63 battalions and a budget line of ₹12,052 crore for 2026-27 later, the order remains unsigned.On Thursday (October 1), then, the force marked its raising day as what it has quietly become: routinely described as the largest counter-insurgency formation in the world and, for a generation of Kashmiris born or brought up after 1990, among the most visible faces of the Indian state, sometimes more visible than the state itself.A force nobody particularly wanted to pay forThe proposal for a dedicated counter-insurgency force went to the government in 1988, and even the question of who raised it has the faintly comic quality of a file that passed through too many desks.A 2017 Defence Ministry release credits General V.N. Sharma. Most histories give the credit to General S.F. Rodrigues, who was chief when the force was actually raised. The name that recurs most consistently, however, is General B.C. Joshi, whose idea it was and who, after becoming chief, pushed its expansion to 36 battalions by 1994, the year he died in office. Its first Director General was Lieutenant General P.C. Mankotia.The original design was a hybrid. Only a quarter of the men were meant to come from the regular Army; the rest would be ex-servicemen and lateral inductees from the paramilitary, somewhat in the manner of the Assam Rifles.That is not what happened. The Rashtriya Rifles became, and remains, an all-Army force: officers and jawans on deputation, drawn on an all-India, all-class basis from virtually every arm and service, serving tenures of roughly thirty months before returning to their parent units.The money was messier still. Since internal security fell under the Home Ministry, the Home Ministry initially paid for the RR. By the time that arrangement ended in 1997, it reportedly owed the Army ₹950 crore for raising and equipping the force. From 1998-99, the Defence Ministry took the bill onto its own books; the allocation that first year was ₹263 crore.The Home Ministry, meanwhile, had questioned whether the force should exist at all, arguing that its creation amounted to accepting that internal rebellion had become a permanent feature of Indian life.It remains one of the more clear-eyed sentences produced by any ministry on Kashmir, and among the more comprehensively ignored.What the borrowed soldiers didThe RR’s finest hour is probably the one almost nobody remembers.In the summer of 1999, while the country watched the ridgelines of Kargil, 26 RR units held the Valley and another three guarded the Banihal and Jawahar Tunnel approaches. Roads remained open. Lines of communication remained usable. The war on the heights could therefore be fought without the Valley unravelling behind it.There is, unfortunately, no battle honour for a highway that stays open.The structure of the force explains much of the method. An RR battalion carries six rifle companies rather than the infantry’s four, leaves much of its heavy weaponry at base and, unlike a regular unit rotating between stations, remains tied to the same terrain: the same district, villages, orchards, roads and families.Five Counter Insurgency Force headquarters — Victor, Kilo, Delta, Romeo and Uniform — divide the territory between them.The rifles, in that sense, are only part of the inventory. The other asset is accumulated memory: which family had a son disappear in 2016, which hillside trail is usable after the snow, which village argument is merely a village argument and which one means somebody ought to pay attention.By the force’s own 2015 tally, it had neutralised 16,368 militants: 8,522 killed, 6,737 apprehended and 1,109 who surrendered.The latter two figures deserve more attention than they usually get. Nearly half the men in that total were either captured alive or surrendered. Counter-insurgency is often narrated through body counts because body counts are simple, but a man who gives up his weapon is, in several respects, the more interesting outcome.By its 27th raising day in 2017, RR personnel had received 7 Ashok Chakras, 34 Kirti Chakras, 238 Shaurya Chakras and 1,637 Sena Medals.Names on the ledgerOne of the more complicated arguments for the RR model was made by a man who had once stood on the other side of it.Nazir Ahmad Wani, from Cheki Ashmuji in Kulgam, had been a militant before surrendering and joining the Territorial Army in 2004. In November 2018, operating with 34 RR at Batagund in Shopian against six heavily armed Hizbul Mujahideen and Lashkar militants, he continued fighting after being mortally wounded and killed two of them.He became the first Kashmiri to receive the Ashok Chakra. His widow, Mahajabeen, accepted it at the Republic Day parade.Five years later, in September 2023, the price was paid in a single morning in the Gadole forests above Kokernag.Colonel Manpreet Singh, commanding 19 RR and four months from the end of his tenure, Major Aashish Dhonchak, who left behind a two-year-old daughter, and Sepoy Pradeep Singh died alongside Deputy Superintendent Humayun Bhat of the J&K Police. Bhat’s father, himself a retired police officer, laid a wreath on his son’s coffin.Two uniforms, one forest. It is worth remembering, especially in the easy shorthand of conversations about Kashmir, that the Kashmiri policeman has spent these decades in the same line of fire.Some names travelled further. Major Mukund Varadarajan of 44 RR became the subject of the Tamil film Amaran in 2024. Others travelled less: Naik Dilwar Khan of 28 RR, killed in Kupwara in July 2024, was awarded the Kirti Chakra the following January.An anniversary piece that mentions the medals must mention something else as well.A force that has operated among civilians under AFSPA for thirty-six years cannot be the sole author of its own report card. Kashmir keeps a ledger too, and not every entry in it is a citation. A country confident about its institutions ought to be capable of reading both without pretending that one makes the other disappear.The quiet handoverThe unwinding has, in fact, already begun, in the manner Indian institutions generally prefer: gradually, administratively and without anybody standing at a lectern to announce that history has changed direction.In 2021, the RR headquarters moved from Delhi to Northern Command in Udhampur, and its chief was downgraded from lieutenant general to major general. A year earlier, after Galwan, Uniform Force had been moved to Ladakh to face a considerably more conventional adversary.After the Pahalgam attack of April 2025, the Defence and Home ministries began discussing the movement of RR battalions out of the hinterland and towards the Line of Control, with the CRPF taking a larger internal-security role. Three CRPF battalions were moved into Udhampur and Kathua as part of that process.Last month brought a more concrete step: around 2,100 CRPF personnel and at least nine CoBRA teams are to take over 21 sensitive locations across those two districts, operating from existing Army camps. Reports have been equally careful to point out that a substantial RR presence will remain.The budget, meanwhile, continues to rise. In May, the Army began procuring 159 bullet-proof troop carriers for RR units, capable of operating at altitudes of up to 5,000 metres.A force preparing to disappear does not usually buy new vehicles.The better description, therefore, is probably redeployment rather than withdrawal: away, slowly, from the orchard and towards the frontier. That is a sensible direction, but nearly everything depends on the pace.Retired officers who support the shift have also cautioned against pulling RR battalions out abruptly, because what the CRPF needs to inherit is not merely a camp. Camps are easy. There are registers, stores, maps, keys and handover notes.Thirty-six years of village-level memory is rather harder to put into a folder. The Army can transfer the barracks. It cannot transfer an informer’s trust.General Joshi built the Rashtriya Rifles as a bridge, meant to carry the state across a crisis for which it had not prepared. Bridges sometimes remain standing long after the emergency that required them, partly because they continue to be useful and partly because institutions, like people, become reluctant to give up arrangements that work.Usefulness is not the same thing as permanence. The most meaningful raising-day gift for the Rashtriya Rifles would therefore not be another parade or another citation. It would be the slow, careful fulfilment of the possibility written into its creation in 1990: that there might come a day when the force was needed less.Not because it had failed, but , in enough places, it had done what it was raised to do.

articles.title: A Nebraska farmer found his father’s 1946 John Deere GM rusting under a tree decades after it left the family; he recognised it by a hand clutch modified after a childhood mishap and restored it
articles.summary: Some family heirlooms sit in attics or pass quietly from one generation to the next.
articles.body: Some family heirlooms sit in attics or pass quietly from one generation to the next. For Nebraska farmer Shelley Bruha, his was a 1946 John Deere GM tractor, an old machine that disappeared from the family decades ago and was eventually found rusting beneath a tree on another Nebraska farm. What gave it away was not a serial number or a familiar paint job. It was a small modification made by his father many years earlier, after a childhood accident involving the tractor’s hand clutch, states an online report by Farm Progress. Scroll down to read the details.A childhood lesson in leverageAccording to the online report, when Bruha was young, he climbed onto his father’s open-station John Deere GM. The tractor’s hand clutch had recently been tightened, leaving the young driver without enough leverage to operate it properly. The result was a frightening ride through a fencerow when Bruha reached the end of a field and could not slow the tractor as intended. His father responded by taking the unusual modification to a local welder. The clutch rod was extended, giving his son enough leverage to operate the mechanism from the driver’s seat. That improvised repair became more than a practical fix. Decades later, it would become the clue that led Bruha back to his family’s lost tractor.A wartime John DeereThe John Deere GM had its own place in American agricultural history. As per the report, introduced in 1942, during the final years of World War II, the 34-horsepower tractor was a wartime version of John Deere’s Model G. It featured electric starting and lights, a 412-cubic-inch engine and a six-speed transmission, giving it improvements over the more basic Model G. Its price was also shaped by wartime controls. The Office of Price Administration regulated the cost of tractors under the Emergency Price Control Act, limiting price increases on models that had not undergone substantial changes during the war.Production of the GM ran from 1942 through 1947, with approximately 13,000 units built. That made it considerably less common than the Model G, which saw production of roughly 64,000 units between 1937 and 1953. Rubber shortages during the war also meant some GM tractors left factories equipped with steel wheels. Later examples were fitted with rubber tires, and today the model has become a sought-after machine among vintage tractor enthusiasts.Found beneath a Nebraska treeAs per the online report, the Bruha family eventually sold its GM, and the tractor spent years working on another farm. Then, decades later, Bruha came across an old John Deere sitting beneath a shade tree on another Nebraska property. The tractor was weathered and rusting, and there was no serial number available to immediately confirm its identity. There was, however, the hand clutch. The extended rod was a detail Bruha remembered from childhood—the modification his father had commissioned after the fencerow incident. It was distinctive enough to connect the neglected tractor with the machine that had once belonged to his family.Back where it belongsBruha eventually brought the tractor back into the family and restored it. The machine now has a life far removed from the working fields where it once earned its keep. Rather than being left beneath a tree to deteriorate, it appears at parades and plow days, where its restored form offers a glimpse into an earlier era of American farming, adds the online report. What began as a simple modification to help a child control a tractor ultimately became the identifying mark that helped reunite an aging machine with the family that first owned it.Images Courtesy: Farm ProgressYou use AI every day. articles.title: Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha picks: Samajwadi Party's master strategy or 'PDA' contradiction?
articles.summary: A 'family' man, a corporate executive, a possible third candidate and a high-stakes numbers game: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha
articles.body: A 'family' man, a corporate executive, a possible third candidate and a high-stakes numbers game: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha strategy has a bit of a test run for the 2027 UP assembly polls?His two picks have an element of continuity and also surprise. But then there is also an element of contradiction vis-à-vis the strong PDA pitch which has been the backbone of his 2027 poll strategy. Little wonder, then, that talk of a third nominee has begun even without the numbers, raising the stakes from a routine Rajya Sabha contest to an early test of Akhilesh's 2027 strategy.For the two sure-shot Rajya Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav has paired a familiar Samajwadi Party face with a distinctly unfamiliar political profile. Alongside his uncle Ram Gopal Yadav, the SP has nominated Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani, a senior Reliance Industries executive whose father, Parimal Nathwani, is a four-time Rajya Sabha MP backed by the BJP-led NDA. The choice immediately puts two very different images of the SP on the same ticket: its established family name and a corporate, professional profile from outside its traditional ecosystem.Nathwani's nomination also raises a larger question about the SP's direction as it prepares for the 2027 assembly election. Is Nathwani's nomination an attempt to expand the SP's political appeal beyond its traditional social base, or does bringing a senior corporate executive into Parliament sit uneasily with a party increasingly building its politics for the 2027 polls around PDA, Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak? The question matters beyond the Rajya Sabha because the SP is simultaneously trying to project itself as the principal challenger to the BJP in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the 2027 assembly election.Why Nathwani?Akhilesh's second nomination is more than a surprise name on a candidate list. His corporate background gives the SP an opportunity to make a political argument it has not traditionally foregrounded. The party can present his candidature as evidence that its appeal is extending beyond its conventional political base and that people from the corporate and professional world now see the party as a credible political force.For a party preparing for 2027, that can also help reinforce a broader pitch around investment, jobs, industry and development alongside its social-justice agenda, which could become a significant part of the BJP and Yogi government's election campaign next year.Akhilesh, in fact, responded to queries over criticism of Nathwani's nomination by invoking Ram Manohar Lohia. "I think you should read about socialism again. I will give you a book by (Ram Manohar) Lohia," he said. He argued that socialist thought also talks about prosperity and equality and said governments across the country seek investment to generate economic growth."This time, it will be Lodhi vs Yogi (Adityanath)," he said on September 30.However, the same choice also produces a very different political reading.Akhilesh's electoral strategy for the 2027 polls has been heavily identified with PDA, and Nathwani is not an obvious representative of the social coalition that phrase describes. That gives the opposition an opening to question why a party seeking votes in the name of backward classes, Dalits and minorities has chosen a senior corporate executive for one of its two Rajya Sabha seats.Mayawati, in fact, used the same charge against the SP. "SP wants votes in the name of PDA, but makes mostly its own family members and big capitalists MPs and MLAs," she said in a post on X.State minister and Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party (SBSP) president Om Prakash Rajbhar also targeted Akhilesh, accusing him of repeatedly changing the framework for PDA. "Akhilesh Yadav keeps changing the PDA formula from time to time. Yesterday, he came up with the formula of a PDA family. 'P' now stands for 'Parivaar'," Rajbhar said, referring to Ram Gopal Yadav. "‘D’ stands for the 'Daulat', referring to Dhani Ram, who is affluent," Rajbhar said."Now, only 'A' remains, and he will bring in some criminal to represent it. The new PDA formula stands for 'Parivaar', 'Daulat' and 'Apradhi'," he added.The BJP, meanwhile, is watching Nathwani's nomination closely but has not mounted a similarly strong direct attack on the choice.The third nomination suspenseThe Uttar Pradesh assembly currently has 396 effective members after seven vacancies, putting the winning quota for a Rajya Sabha seat at 37 first-preference votes. The BJP has 255 MLAs, while the SP has 101 and Congress has two. The BJP's alliance partners include Apna Dal (S), RLD, SBSP and Nishad Party, giving the ruling camp a substantial numerical advantage. Broadly, the BJP-led camp is positioned to take the larger share of the 10 seats, while the SP-Congress combination has enough strength for two.The problem begins with the third candidate. The SP would need roughly nine additional first-preference votes to reach the quota for a third seat. That means Akhilesh cannot rely only on his existing alliance strength. He would have to attract support from outside it, potentially through smaller parties, independents or legislators willing to cross-vote.The suspense over that third candidate has now become central to the contest. SP MP Virendra Singh has said the party will field a third candidate, with the name to be decided and the nomination filed by October 5. Singh has also claimed that several BJP MLAs seeking SP tickets for the 2027 elections are in touch with the party.Akhilesh, meanwhile, has continued to leave room for political manoeuvring. Earlier in the day he described the Rajya Sabha election as "the time for coming together" and said it offered an opportunity to forget past mistakes and stand united with others on matters of principle.A day earlier, when asked whether the SP would field a third candidate, he declined to confirm the party's plans and said: "The BJP can do anything. They can field nine or even 10 candidates."The BJP, meanwhile, has made its own claims about SP legislators. Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya has said that 25 SP MLAs are in contact with the BJP and warned that the party would "surprise" the SP.A rehearsal for 2027This Rajya Sabha election, along with the immediate parliamentary tally, will ultimately be about a strategic stress-test for 2027.In fielding Nathwani, Akhilesh Yadav is executing a high-stakes balancing act: attempting to reposition the Samajwadi Party as a pragmatic, investment-friendly government-in-waiting, without alienating the core PDA base that forms its electoral backbone. It is a gamble that risks handing opponents cheap ideological ammunition in exchange for broader institutional credibility and expanded corporate outreach.Whether this move is remembered as a masterstroke of political expansion or a self-inflicted ideological contradiction will not be decided in the corridors of the Rajya Sabha. It will be decided by how effectively Akhilesh manages the cross-currents - maintaining the confidence of his grassroots voters while proving that his vision for Uttar Pradesh can accommodate both social justice and corporate capital. The upcoming floor vote, and the potential fight for a third seat, will offer the first real glimpse of whether that strategy can hold.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Rahul Gandhi demands CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation as protests erupt in Delhi, Mumbai
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Friday demanded the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Friday demanded the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as opposition parties, student groups and civil society organisations held protests in Delhi and Mumbai over alleged irregularities in the electoral-roll revision exercise.In a post on X on Gandhi Jayanti, the Raebareli MP said thousands of young people were protesting peacefully against what he called “vote theft” and alleged that hundreds had been detained.“Today is Gandhi Jayanti. And today, thousands of young people are on the streets against vote theft - peacefully, without violence, exercising their constitutional rights. Their demand is clear: Gyanesh Kumar must resign. Save democracy,” the Congress leader said.He alleged that the response of the “Modi-Shah government” had been to detain protesters.“And the Modi-Shah government's response? Boys and girls are being dragged off the streets. Hundreds are in custody. Their only crime is that they dared to question vote theft,” he said.Former Congress president also invoked Mahatma Gandhi’s teachings on non-violence and truth, saying, “Bapu taught us exactly this - speak the truth, fight peacefully. And that's what scares this government the most.”“Because a lathi can stop a crowd, but not a question. Gyanesh Kumar will go. And the system that put him there will go too,” he added.Around 700 detained in DelhiOpposition parties and student organisations attempted to gather near Jantar Mantar in Delhi, with the AAP, All India Students' Association (AISA), Students' Federation of India (SFI), National Students' Union of India (NSUI), Indian Youth Congress (IYC) and other youth groups demanding Kumar’s resignation.According to news agency PTI, around 700 protesters were detained by Delhi Police. Protesters were stopped at several points, including Firoz Shah Road and Ashoka Road, as they tried to proceed towards Jantar Mantar.AAP leaders Saurabh Bharadwaj, Atishi and Sanjeev Jha were among those detained, while Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Singh was stopped on his way to the protest. Internet services were suspended in central Delhi and entry and exit gates at 12 metro stations, including Rajiv Chowk and Central Secretariat, were closed as part of security arrangements.SFI general secretary Aishe Ghosh said activists of the SFI and Democratic Youth Federation of India were also detained. AAP leaders alleged that police action would not stop their campaign.“We are protesting because the EC is responsible for protecting the sanctity of every vote. When questions are being raised within the commission itself over decisions concerning the electoral roll, the country deserves answers and accountability,” IYC president Uday Bhanu Chib said, according to PTI.Protests in Mumbai and questions over SIRProtests were also held at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park, where thousands attended a demonstration organised by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and other groups seeking Kumar’s resignation.CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke warned of “Jantar Mantar 2.0” if Kumar did not step down, while party leader Ajinkya Shinde demanded his resignation and criminal proceedings. The CJP also called for the freezing of the 2025 voter lists and the abolition of the 2023 law governing the appointment of election commissioners.Dipke made several allegations concerning voter deletions and additions across states, including Maharashtra, Delhi, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. These claims were made by him during the protest and were not independently established in the supplied reports.The protests came after an Indian Express report claimed that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months on decisions and procedures linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise and other electoral matters.The Election Commission rejected the suggestion that these objections represented institutional dissent, saying operational queries, inputs and suggestions during the draft stage were part of its normal administrative and decision-making process.The ECI said decisions on the SIR schedule were unanimous.The opposition’s campaign is expected to continue, with further programmes planned, including one on October 6 and a major rally in Delhi on November 1.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: France paid people to kill Mediterranean dolphins in 1865 to protect fisheries; a study calls it the first recorded dolphin bounty
articles.summary: France paid people to kill Mediterranean dolphins in 1865 to protect fisheries; a study calls it the first recorded dolphin bounty
articles.body: In 1865, the French government began paying people to kill dolphins in the Mediterranean Sea, offering twenty-five francs for each animal. Officials introduced the reward to protect fisheries, because fishing communities believed dolphins were emptying the sea of fish and tearing their nets. A major review of bounty programmes, published in 2026, identifies it as the first recorded dolphin bounty. The story is an example of how people have tried to solve economic problems by paying citizens to kill wildlife, and of how often such schemes have produced consequences that nobody planned for. Here is what happened and what history teaches.How the 1865 French dolphin bounty in the Mediterranean Sea paid twenty-five francs per animalThe French scheme worked like a classic bounty. The government offered a fixed cash payment, twenty-five francs, to anyone who killed a dolphin in the Mediterranean. The aim was to reduce dolphin numbers and, with them, the harm that fishing communities blamed on the animals. The review titled ‘Society’s struggle with unwanted species: what centuries of history reveal about species bounty programs’ documents the scheme does not report how many dolphins were killed in France, so the scale of the slaughter remains unclear.Why fishing communities blamed dolphins for falling fish stocks and damaged netsThe researchers explain that perceived threats to local economies drove the bounty. Fishers saw dolphins as competitors for dwindling fish and as a danger to expensive nets. The word "perceived" matters here, because the review describes these bounties as targeting reported or believed damage, which was not always measured or proven. The review lists the dolphins in question as the species found in the Mediterranean, the common dolphin, Risso's dolphin, the striped dolphin and the common bottlenose dolphin.Dolphin bounties spread to Italy, Croatia and JapanFrance was not alone. The review also records dolphin bounties in Italy, Croatia, and Japan. In Italy in 1889, the government paid for each dolphin killed and authorised experimental use of bomb guns. Protecting fisheries was the common thread, the same motive that led to bounties on seals, pelicans, cormorants and even bald eagles in other parts of the world.What a global review reveals about killing wildlife for cashThe dolphin bounty appears in the first global assessment of species bounty programmes, led by Julian D. Olden and colleagues and published in the journal npj Biodiversity on 30 May 2026. Drawing on eight centuries of evidence, the team found at least 283 species targeted across 449 programmes in 60 countries. Mammals made up just over a third of the species, birds just over a third, and fish about one in nine.Marine animals were a small minority, around 8.5 per cent of the species, which makes the dolphin bounties unusual. The authors caution that their count is conservative because sources in languages other than English are not fully represented.Why bounty schemes often fail and shifting public opinionThe review draws five lessons, and several apply to any bounty:Motives vary: Programmes have been launched for economic, ecological and public health reasons, and fisheries protection is one of the economic motives.Design varies: Some schemes had clear goals and monitoring, while others simply counted kills.Unintended consequences are common: Bounties can kill non-target species or even help the target species recover its numbers.Fraud happens: In Hanoi in 1902, hunters cut the tails off rats and released them to breed, and in colonial Delhi people reportedly bred cobras for the reward.Public opinion shifts: Support often fades as animal welfare concerns grow, and one Australian pelican bounty ended abruptly after public outcry.Lessons from the dolphin bounty for modern wildlife and fisheries managementThe review notes a striking reversal over time. Of 260 animal species once subject to bounties, 22 are now classed as at risk or extinct by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and another 16 are near threatened. The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, is the most famous casualty, driven to extinction in 1936 with a bounty as a primary contributor.The authors do not claim there is a single answer about the future of bounties. Supporters see them as one useful tool, while critics say they can be costly, ineffective and a distraction from deeper causes such as habitat loss, pollution and climate change. The 1865 French dolphin bounty shows how long this debate has been running.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Carney to meet Erdogan in Turkey amid US trade tensions, seeks new markets beyond Washington: Report
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkey this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan, in what would be the first dedicated bilateral
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkey this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan, in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources familiar with the plans told Reuters.The two leaders are expected to discuss free-trade negotiations launched on the sidelines of a Nato summit in Ankara in July, as well as potential cooperation in energy and defence, one of the sources said.Canadian and Turkish trade ministers agreed this week to accelerate the negotiations ahead of the proposed meeting, two sources told Reuters. The sources did not disclose the dates or agenda of Carney’s planned visit.The trip would be the latest step in Carney’s efforts to diversify Canada’s trade and diplomatic ties and reduce its dependence on the United States, its largest trading partner. The effort follows the collapse of trade talks with Washington in August.Carney’s office and Erdogan’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Carney seeks to diversify Canada's trade tiesCarney has pledged to double Canada’s non-US trade over the next decade and has moved to strengthen relations with several countries, including China and India, with which Canada has had strained ties in the past.His outreach has placed less emphasis on human rights concerns than that of previous Canadian governments, as he seeks to build economic partnerships amid US tariffs. Polls have shown strong support among Canadians for efforts to reinforce the country’s economy.Erdogan, who has led Turkey for 23 years, is also seeking new markets and partnerships for the country’s defence industry, which has expanded in recent years. Turkey is looking to attract investment and cooperation in sectors including energy, infrastructure and mining.Rights groups have criticised Erdogan’s government over its crackdown on the political opposition since 2024. Erdogan has said an independent judiciary is investigating the opposition and rejected claims that the cases are politically motivated.Human rights concerns in TurkeyWestern countries have become less vocal about Turkey’s human rights record as Ankara has emerged as a defence-industrial power and a key partner in efforts to counter Russian aggression, Reuters reported.A wave of arrests and restrictions targeting Turkey’s LGBTQ+ community began last month. The government has said the measures are part of an investigation aimed at protecting children and family values. Rights groups and some European officials have criticised the actions.The planned visit would mark a rare standalone bilateral trip by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. No Canadian leader is known to have made such a visit in recent decades, although Canadian prime ministers have met Erdogan and other Turkish leaders on the sidelines of multilateral gatherings, including Nato and G20 summits hosted by Turkey.Trade talks and defence cooperationCarney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement during the Nato leaders’ summit in July.Turkey also agreed that month to join Canada’s Defence Security and Resilience Bank as one of the 10 founding members of Carney’s proposed multilateral institution for middle powers.The two countries’ trade ministers met in June and discussed expanding cooperation in renewable and nuclear energy, according to a Canadian government statement. Aerospace, defence and security were also identified as potential areas for new partnerships.Turkey has been exploring options for building its second and third nuclear power plants. It has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis, South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation and China’s State Power Investment Corporation. Russia’s Rosatom is building Turkey’s first nuclear power plant.An AtkinsRealis executive told Reuters this year that the company expected Turkey to complete an early review of its CANDU reactor technology following an information exchange. The review could lead to concrete discussions about a potential bid to build a plant, the executive said.Canada and Turkey took steps to improve bilateral ties in 2024, when Ottawa removed weapons-export controls on Turkey. The restrictions had included controls on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of countries.Bilateral trade remains limitedDespite the push to expand economic ties, trade between Canada and Turkey remains modest.Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada’s total merchandise trade in 2025, worth C$4.34 billion ($3.05 billion), compared with about C$1 trillion in trade with the United States, according to Statistics Canada data cited by Reuters.Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey. Its imports from Turkey include medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewellery.The proposed visit comes as both countries seek to broaden their economic and strategic partnerships. For Canada, Turkey offers a potential partner beyond its traditional trade relationships, while Ankara is seeking investment and access to new markets for its energy, infrastructure and defence sectors.You use AI every day. articles.title: From Shiv-on to off: Musk’s half-Indian partner goes into ex space
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Elon Musk has apparently discovered that even a man trying to repopulate civilisation can run into the oldest problem
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Elon Musk has apparently discovered that even a man trying to repopulate civilisation can run into the oldest problem in human relationships: boredom.Shivon Zilis, the Indian-origin, Canada-born Neuralink executive and mother of four of Musk’s children, announced on Thursday that her romantic relationship with the billionaire was over -- and suggested that the separation came rather suddenly.“It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes,” Zilis wrote on X, the platform owned by her partner. She said she was grateful to have shown Musk “how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” adding that she hoped they could remain “great friends and coparents.”“God speed, Elon, the world is lucky to have you,” she concluded with grace.The timing gives a slightly surreal resonance to two recent occasions on which Musk went out of his way to mention Zilis's Indian ancestry. In a conversation with Indian entrepreneur and podcaster Nikhil Kamath last December, Musk volunteered: “My partner Shivon, she is half Indian. I do not know if you know that.” He added that one of their sons had the middle name Sekhar, after Nobel laureate and astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Zilis, he explained, grew up in Canada after having been given up for adoption as a baby; her biological father was apparently an Indian exchange student.More recently, in a July interview with The Economist, the subject came up again -- this time as Musk's response to a question about accusations that he is racist. “My partner is... half Indian and I have four children with her. You know, one of them was named after a famous Indian physicist. So I would say I'm not racist,” Musk told editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes.Zilis was not merely an obscure romantic footnote in Musk's complicated family tree. She is a prominent technology executive who worked at OpenAI before joining Musk's companies and became an executive at Neuralink. She and Musk had twins, Strider Sekhar and Azure, in November 2021, followed by daughter Arcadia in February 2024 and son Seldon Lycurgus, whose birth was announced in February 2025.Musk once explained that Strider Sekhar was named partly for The Lord of the Rings character Aragorn and partly for Chandrasekhar -- making the boy perhaps the only person in the Musk dynasty whose name simultaneously evokes Middle-earth and a summit.Shivon was also visibly part of Musk's public life in recent months. When PM Narendra Modi visited Washington in February 2025, Zilis accompanied Musk to his meeting with Modi at Blair House, across from the White House, along with their children. The photographs of Musk, Zilis, Modi and the children gave the otherwise quiet relationship an unusually public Indian connection.Musk's family arrangements are, by now, sufficiently elaborate to require a spreadsheet. He was married three times to two women: author Justine Wilson, his first wife, and actress Talulah Riley, whom he married twice. With Wilson he had six children, including twins and triplets; their first son, Nevada, died as an infant. He subsequently had three children with musician Grimes — one named with an odd combination of alphabet and numbers, Exa Dark Siderael, and Techno Mechanicus. Zilis brought the tally to four children, while conservative influencer Ashley St. Clair has also said Musk fathered her son Romulus. Publicly reported totals now stand at 14 children.The numbers are not accidental. Musk has repeatedly warned about declining birth rates and described population collapse as one of civilisation's greatest dangers. After the birth of his twins with Zilis became public, he declared on X that he was doing his best to help with the “underpopulation crisis.”There is also an unmistakably Muskian irony to the latest development. The man who worries that humanity isn't making enough babies has demonstrated that producing children may be considerably easier than maintaining the relationship with the person producing them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sowmiya launches liquor-free Tamil Nadu movement, calls for imposition of total prohibition
articles.summary: Dharmapuri MLA Sowmiya Anbumani launches “Madhu Illa Tamilagam” liquor-free Tamil Nadu movement, urging total prohibition and citing alcohol harm data.
articles.body: Chennai: Pasumai Thaayagam president and Dharmapuri MLA Sowmiya Anbumani has launched a social awareness movement titled “Madhu Illa Tamilagam” (Liquor-Free Tamil Nadu) in a simple function in Chennai on Friday. She released a comprehensive manifesto detailing the devastating socio-economic, medical, and generational impacts of alcoholism across the state during the launch of the movement.The campaign issues a clarion call for the immediate phase-out of liquor sales in Tamil Nadu, urging citizens across caste, religious, and political lines to unite on a war footing to eradicate alcohol consumption. According to data published in the movement’s declaration charter, alcohol abuse has escalated into an existential threat to public health and family stability in Tamil Nadu.An estimated 80 lakh people in Tamil Nadu consume alcohol, with nearly 54 lakh individuals requiring medical intervention for addiction. While Tamil Nadu accounts for 5.5% of India’s population, it contributes a disproportionate 16% to national alcohol sales, three times higher than average. State liquor revenue has increased 14-fold over the past 25 years, while sales volume grew by 4.8 times, said the charter.The charter said 90% of families with alcohol-dependent members live in severe poverty, while 85% suffer under heavy debt burdens, often lacking funds even for basic healthcare. The economic loss to the public due to alcohol consumption is three times higher than the revenue the state govt earns from its sale, it said.It said domestic violence surges from 28% in non-drinking households to 81% in families with alcohol dependency, a three-fold increase. Tamil Nadu records the highest rate of widowed or abandoned women in India (11.6% compared to the national average of 5.5%). Tamil Nadu accounts for 14% of India’s total road accidents, with drunk driving being a primary factor. articles.title: ‘Clear tram tracks of illegal parking’
articles.summary: Illegal parking on Kolkata tram tracks is stranding trams on Esplanade-Gariahat and Esplanade-Shyambazar routes; operators urge stricter enforcement.
articles.body: Kolkata: Vehicles being parked illegally on tram tracks, especially at night, are posing a hurdle for trams.At a time when the new govt assures of revival of tram networks, operators request the authorities and police to keep the tracks free. At present, trams run on only two routes—Esplanade-Gariahat and Esplanade-Shyambazar. Operators pointed out that they faced trouble especially on central Kolkata stretches, such as Lenin Sarani, Rafi Ahmed Kidwai Road and Nirmal Chunder Street.They said motorists and mini-truck drivers parked their vehicles on tram tracks and disappeared at night, as a result of which they got stranded. On Thursday night, a Gariahat-bound tram remained stuck for nearly half-an-hour between Chandni Market and Wellington Square on Lenin Sarani as a private car blocked the tracks and the driver could not be found for several minutes, said an operator. Commuters were forced to alight and join the tram driver and conductor in search for the elusive motorist.“Taxis, mini trucks and vans are regularly being left behind on tram tracks. Often, the drivers cannot be found anywhere and we have to call up Lalbazar traffic control room to get the tracks cleared,” said a conductor at the Gariahat depot.Beckbagan resident Tanmoy Bhattacharya who was on board the stranded Gariahat-bound tram on Esplanade-Gariahat route on Thursday night said, “I boarded the tram from the Tipu Sultan mosque stop. Within 200m, it came to a halt as a car was parked in front. The driver kept ringing the bell but to no avail. We looked for the driver but could not be found. After waiting for 20 minutes, I had to look for an auto. I request the govt to take action against such illegal parking on tram tracks.”Ravi Inder Singh, principal secretary of the state transport department, told TOI: “We will take up the matter with the authority concerned. Trams should always get the right of way. We are working to revive the tram networks.”In the past, members of Calcutta Tram Users’ Association lodged several police complaints but no action was taken, said Souvik Mukherjee, a member of HC-appointed Calcutta Tram Welfare Committee. “Illegal parking on tracks is regular during the day as well. articles.title: Noida Authority plans 4-floor digital library in Sector 52
articles.summary: Noida Authority to build Rs 8.29-crore, 4-floor digital public library in Sector 52 with 300 seats, computers, Wi-Fi, seminar room; ready by 2027 end.
articles.body: Noida: From bookshelves stocked with titles across subjects to computers offering access to digital resources, Noida’s upcoming public library in Sector 52 is envisioned as a space where students and readers can learn, prepare and explore under one roof.Noida Authority is set to build the four-storey facility in Block B of Sector 52, spread across 3,000 square metres, including the ground floor, with a seating capacity of 300. Apart from books on different subjects, the library will house study material for major competitive examinations, making it a resource centre for students preparing for various entrance and recruitment tests.The Rs 8.29-crore facility will have a dedicated computer section with large screens, printers, internet access and LAN networking. A seminar room and cafeteria are also part of the plan, along with air conditioning, clean drinking water and security arrangements.“In addition to books, students will have access to a dedicated computer section within the library. Facilities for internet access and digital content will be provided,” said SP Singh, general manager (Civil), Noida Authority.LED lighting, acoustic false ceilings, illuminated signage, CCTV surveillance and landscaped outdoor spaces will add to the facility. Entry will be free for students, while the library will be operated through a corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative.Authority has finalised the architectural design and issued a construction tender. The project is expected to take a year, with the library likely to be ready by the end of 2027. Another similar facility is also planned in a sector yet to be identified.“We want a similar facility like the Coforge Library in Noida for Sector 52 library. For this, we will give a contract for it to be operated through a CSR drive. The final modalities regarding its operation and management will be determined in due course,” Singh said.Noida already has Coforge Public Library in Sector 59, a CSR initiative by Coforge Limited that offers over 10,000 books and digital access. Similar facilities run by the company are located in Gurgaon, Hyderabad and Delhi.While residents have welcomed the proposed library, they have also flagged concerns over the likely increase in visitors and the pressure this could place on neighbourhood infrastructure.“If such a large public library is built inside Sector 52, a significant number of people from outside the sector will also visit it. This could lead to several practical problems, including parking shortages, increased traffic, security concerns, overcrowding, cleanliness issues, and other related challenges. articles.title: Trichy corpn initiates study for skywalks under PPP
articles.summary: Trichy Corporation revives skywalk plan via PPP at two city locations; Rs 5 lakh sanctioned for DFR to identify viable sites and improve pedestrian safety.
articles.body: Trichy: A decade after its attempts to develop skywalks for safe commute of pedestrians failed to take off, Trichy corporation has revived the proposal through public private partnership (PPP) mode at two locations in the city. The civic body has sanctioned Rs 5 lakh inviting suitable agencies to prepare a detailed feasibility report (DFR) for skywalks.According to the survey conducted by the town and country planning department, only 68% of road network in the city have footpaths on both sides, while 12% have none at all. The central business district (CBD) areas comprising Cantonment, Thillai Nagar, Chathiram bus stand, and Singarathope have severe vehicular - pedestrian conflicts. Railway junction to Central bus stand junction stretch alone handles around one lakh vehicles a day, but people commuting between two transit hubs on foot lack facilities for the safe commute.“We have received a directive from the department of municipal administration (DMA) to develop pedestrian-friendly infrastructures. A tender has been floated to identify an agency to prepare a feasibility report. The agency will list out viable locations, and we will scrutinize and choose based on the need,” an official said. PPP model is most likely to be explored for funding the infrastructure, and the study will be completed in a month.In 2015-16, the local body proposed two pedestrian foot overbridges at Rs 1.9 crore in Chathiram bus stand and Melapudur, but they didn’t materialize. This time, officials said that a suitable financial model will be explored to make skywalks a reality as the city’s commercial streets and transit hubs are totally devoid of pedestrian infrastructure.“Panjapur bus terminus of late records mass movement of students crossing the busy Trichy-Madurai highway in a risky manner. Many roads within the city such as railway junction and MGMGH pose serious threats for pedestrians crossing them. articles.title: Man held for cheating 10 people of Rs 5.3 lakh in fake job case
articles.summary: Trichy police arrest Musiri man for allegedly cheating 10 job seekers of Rs 5.3 lakh by promising assistant jobs at district collectorate; probe on.
articles.body: Trichy: Sessions court police on Thursday arrested a 28-year-old man from Musiri on charges of cheating 10 job seekers of Rs 5.3 lakh under the pretext of arranging jobs for them at the Trichy district collectorate.Police identified the accused as J Surya of Thiruthiyamalai. He initially promised T Sathishkumar, 52, from Uyyakondan Thirumalai, to fetch an assistant job in Trichy district collectorate for his daughter and collected Rs 50,000 from the man. Similarly, nine other job seekers transferred Rs 50,000 each for the assistant job. Separately, he received a sum of Rs 32,000 under the pretext of conducting medical check-ups for the job seekers.Some of the victims handed over the money to Surya behind the district collectorate between May 25 and June 3. As Surya neither arranged for jobs nor returned the money, the victims lodged a complaint with police.
